point.en: the paper that proves the train, not you
point.exp:
Trains are late sometimes. What is unusual is not that — it is what happens next.

If your train is delayed by roughly five minutes or more, the railway issues a 遅延証明書, a certificate of delay. You do not have to ask anybody for it. Staff hand them out at the gate on bad mornings, and every major operator posts them on its website, normally covering the last forty-five days including today. You take a photo of it, or print it, and you give it to your employer or your school.

That is the mechanism. Here is why it earns a lesson.

**The certificate does not prove you were on the train.** Read the small print on any operator's page and it says so directly: it certifies the maximum delay on that LINE, in that TIME BAND. Not your individual train. Not that you were a passenger. Anybody could download it, including somebody who was still asleep.

So it is not evidence, and it was never meant to be. It is a document that lets both sides stop discussing the matter. Your lateness now has a cause with a name and a piece of paper attached; your manager has something to put in a file; and nobody has to hold a conversation about whether you left the house on time. The paper's job is social rather than evidential — which is a considerably more interesting fact than the story about Japanese punctuality you were probably told before you arrived.

Some operators round in ways that tell you something. Kintetsu issues in five-minute units, rounding up, and anything past an hour is certified simply as 「61分以上」 — beyond a point, the exact number stops mattering to anyone.

**The grammar here is this step's, and it is not decoration.** A morning like this is made almost entirely of time's edges:

九時までに着かなければなりません — the deadline you are about to miss. までに.
今、出るところです — the moment you are standing in. ところ.
駅に着いたばかりです — only just arrived. ばかり.
遅れている間に、連絡しました — the gap you can still use. 間に.

Four patterns, one bad morning, and the fourth is the one that saves you. 連絡しないで来ました — arriving without having sent word — is what turns a train delay into a problem, and ないで is in this step for exactly that reason.

⚠️ One caution about the thing everybody says. Japanese rail punctuality is high by international standards, and the certificate system exists BECAUSE of it: a delay is unusual enough to be worth documenting at all. That is not the same claim as Japan being a punctual culture, which flattens a great deal. What is fair to say is narrower and more useful — in workplaces and schools, lateness is treated as something that requires an account, and the system has produced a standard form for giving one.
ex: 九時までに着かなければなりません。
I have to be there by nine — までに, the deadline.
I'm just leaving now — ところ, the moment itself.
遅れている間に、会社に連絡しました。
I let the office know while it was held up.
